name: React component library (npm)
description: A React component library for npm: TypeScript, Rollup, CSS Modules, Vitest. Built, type-checked, tested, packed and installed into a scratch project before it counts as done. Publishing is always your own step.

node.what: Node.js, the program that builds and tests the library.
how: Install the current LTS version from https://nodejs.org, then close and reopen the terminal. Check with:  node --version

npm.what: npm, the package manager that comes with Node.js; it installs the library's tooling and builds the package that gets published.
how: It is installed together with Node.js (see node above). Check with:  npm --version

rules.rule: Do no needless work and use only the memory, network, storage and startup time the feature needs: no repeated identical work, no loop over everything, no polling where an event exists, nothing loaded that is not shown, no unbounded read, query or cache, and everything opened (connection, listener, timer, file) is released. It must still behave when the data or the number of users is a hundred times larger.
rules.why: Slow, hungry software costs every user time and money, and what works with ten rows and one user fails at ten thousand.
rules.plain: The app stays fast and light, and keeps working when there is a lot more data or many more people.

rules.rule: No secrets (passwords, API keys, tokens, connection strings) in source code or committed config.
rules.why: Secrets in code end up in git history and leak, and cannot be un-leaked.
rules.plain: Passwords and keys must come from settings, never be written into the code.
rules.good: const token = env.REGISTRY_TOKEN; // read from the environment, never written in the code

rules.rule: Only files inside the design's declared scope may change.
rules.why: Unplanned changes are where regressions hide. Enforced by the engine on the diff.
rules.plain: The developer may only change the parts of the project this change is about.

rules.rule: Every requirement is proven by at least one test that names it.
rules.why: Untested requirements are guesses. Enforced by the engine when the build report is accepted.
rules.plain: Everything you asked for must have a test proving it works.

rules.rule: What the library exports (UI/index.ts) changes only when the design says so. A removed or changed export, prop or type is a breaking change: it is listed in docs/breaking-changes.md and the version is bumped to match.
rules.why: Everyone who installed the library depends on its public surface; an accidental change breaks their apps on the next update.
rules.plain: Changing what the library offers to other people's apps is a decision, written down, never a side effect.

rules.rule: package.json has an "exports" map with "types", "import" and "require" entries for the files in dist/, and the types resolve under both module systems (proven by attw and publint).
rules.why: A library can build and pass its own tests and still be broken for the people who install it: the wrong file loads, or there are no types.
rules.plain: The package must work when other people install it, not just on your machine.

rules.rule: Only dist/ and the documents meant for readers are published (the "files" list), and the packed library installs into a scratch project and imports under both CommonJS and ES modules.
rules.why: Tests and source files in the package leak work in progress and make installs slower; an import that only works in the repository is not a library.
rules.plain: What goes on npm is exactly what you meant, and it really can be installed and used.

rules.rule: react, react-dom and every other peer dependency are external to the bundle (including react/jsx-runtime), declared in peerDependencies with a range, and never in dependencies.
rules.why: A second copy of React inside the library breaks hooks in the app that uses it; a bundled JSX runtime breaks apps on another React version.
rules.plain: The library borrows React from the app that uses it instead of carrying its own copy.

rules.rule: The built bundle starts with "use client" and the package is marked free of side effects ("sideEffects": false, or a list of the CSS files), so Next.js App Router apps can import it and bundlers can drop what is unused.
rules.why: Without the banner, a component that uses state fails to import in a server component; without the flag, apps carry the whole library.
rules.plain: The library works in Next.js apps and does not make apps bigger than needed.

rules.rule: The built library stays within its size budget (.size-limit.json). Raising the budget is a decision recorded with the change, never done to make a check pass.
rules.why: Every kilobyte is paid by every app that installs the library, on every page load.
rules.plain: The library has a weight limit so it never slowly becomes heavy for the apps that use it.

rules.rule: Build for data that grows a hundred times: no work in render that scales with the data (sorting, filtering, mapping huge arrays) without memoization; lists that can be long are paged or virtualized; effects and listeners clean up; no state that grows without bound.
rules.why: Libraries are used on data the author never imagined. A component that is fine with ten rows and unusable with ten thousand is a bug in the library.
rules.plain: Components must stay fast when the amount of data is much larger than in your examples.

rules.rule: Adding, removing or upgrading a dependency, a peer dependency or a tool version is a decision with a reason recorded in the design. Prefer no new dependency; if one is needed, prefer a small one that can be a peer.
rules.why: Dependencies are the library's weight and risk, and they are inherited by every app that installs it.
rules.plain: Nothing new is added to the library's dependencies without a stated reason.

rules.rule: Components support light, dark and system themes through CSS variables, size everything in rem (px only for borders), are keyboard-operable with correct ARIA roles and labels, and are designed for small screens first.
rules.why: A component library is judged by how it behaves in other people's apps, for every user, on every device.
rules.plain: Components look right in light and dark mode, work with a keyboard and a screen reader, and fit small screens.

rules.rule: Every feature, prop and breaking change is documented where readers look: README.md (a first working example), docs/examples.md (recipes), docs/features.md, docs/api.md, docs/configuration.md, docs/development.md and docs/breaking-changes.md, each linking to the previous and next page.
rules.why: A library nobody can figure out does not get used; documentation that lags the code is wrong documentation.
rules.plain: Anything new is explained in the docs with a working example, in the same change.

rules.rule: No debugging leftovers (console.log, console.debug, debugger) in the library's source.
rules.why: Debug output leaks data into other people's consoles and cannot be switched off by the people who installed the library.
rules.plain: Leftover debugging code has to be removed before the change is done.
rules.good: export function format(value: number) { return value.toFixed(2); }

checks.command: echo Not set up in this project: attw and publint are not installed, so nothing checks that the package works for everyone who installs it. && exit 78

startup.title: The packed library installs and imports
startup.ready: The library was packed, installed into an empty project, and imported under both CommonJS and ES modules, with only the intended files published and React kept out of the bundle.
startup.blocked: The packed library does not install or import cleanly, or it would publish files it should not, or it carries its own copy of React. See what the check printed.
startup.notRun: The installed-library check could not run here (it is not set up in this project yet, or there is no internet connection to install into a scratch project), so the library has not been proven to work for the people who install it.
